raw_response:
I've been working this land since I was a teenager, following what my father taught me and watching what the neighbors do. Quzhou is wheat and corn country — has been my whole life. The soil here is okay, not great, but it grows grain. I've got about 8 mu. Every year it's the same: put wheat in before the cold comes, pull it in June, then rush to get corn in the ground before July.

I buy my wheat seed from the county co-op, the improved kind — Jimai or similar. Same with corn, I use hybrid seeds now, have been for about ten years. They yield better. I know how much fertilizer to put down from watching my father and from what the neighbors use. I put down more at the base before planting, then add urea when the wheat starts shooting up in spring. For corn I throw in fertilizer at planting and again when it's knee high. Water is the worry here — I pump from the well, pay for electricity, try not to irrigate too much but I don't let the crops dry out either. Wheat needs water four times to be safe. Corn can manage with less.

For pests, I spray when I see something or when other farmers in the village start spraying — usually twice a season is enough.

I don't change what works. This is what I'll do again this year.

decision.reasoning_summary: I farm 8 mu in Quzhou County using the standard winter wheat and summer maize double-cropping rotation that has been practiced in this region for generations. I plant improved wheat varieties from the county co-op in October after rotary tillage and base fertilization, irrigate four times through the season, apply urea topdressing in spring, and harvest in June. I immediately direct-seed hybrid maize into the stubble with no tillage, apply fertilizer twice, irrigate twice, and harvest in late September. Fertilizer rates follow what my father used and what neighbors apply — roughly 20 kg N per mu for each crop. This system is the only viable livelihood on this land and I see no reason to change it.
